newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan ready to prop up yen, but loath to alter trend.
newsitem.headline: Japan ready to prop up yen, but loath to alter trend.

text.p: Japanese authorities appear eager to let some steam out of the dollar's rally but would be happy to see a gentle landing that keeps the U.S. currency on a firm trend against the yen, traders said on Thursday.

They also said that dollar-selling intervention is on the cards, especially after strong messages from Japanese officials about the yen's fall and Washington's growing worries over a renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus.
But pushing the yen sharply higher would be inconsistent with current economic policies and also hamper the success of its planned "Big Bang" financial market reforms, they said.

"Intervention aimed at pushing the dollar back into a 120-125 yen range would be possible before the G7 (Group of Seven) nations' meeting later this month, but further selling of dollars below that level would be pointless," said Kazunori Iida, manager at the foreign exchange department at Nissho Iwai Corp.
Finance ministers and central bankers of rich nations are scheduled to meet in Washington ahead of the IMF meeting starting on April 28.

The dollar was at around 125.70 yen in late Tokyo on Thursday after rising as high as 127.17 yen recently. The dollar has retraced more than 50 percent from its post-war record low of 79.75 yen in April 1995.

On Wednesday, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official, Eisuke Sakakibara, said the yen's recent tumble has been overdone and he proclaimed he would "win" in any intervention battle with the market.
One reason the markets are nervous is that Japan, with external reserves standing of $219 billion, is well-armed to manipulate the market.

However, Nissho Iwai's Iida said other important policies, such as rock-bottom interest rates and a belt-tightening fiscal stance, would continue to work against intervention to push the dollar down against the yen.
On a longer-term basis, keeping a weak yen would be vital to luring foreign capital into Japan and making financial reforms here successful.
Analysts said Japan expects such foreign money not only to help revive Japan's financial and real-estate sectors but also to offset possible Japanese capital flow overseas.
"It will be necessary for Japan to maintain the yen on a soft trend over the next one or two years to lure foreign capital," said Takuma Kurosawa, chief manager at Mitsubishi Trust and Banking.
"Therefore, the authorities will have no intention of reversing the weak yen trend," he added.
They said the government is concerned that yen volatility will serve to discourage foreign investment just when Japan is launching its drive to get back its role as a financial centre.
Analysts said the sweeping reforms, combined with a weak yen and low interest rates, would provide foreigners with strong incentives to acquire Japanese assets and get a business foothold here.
